claim: Cdc48 is a AAA+ ATPase that plays an essential role for many cellular processes in eukaryotic cells.
source: Cdc48 is a AAA+ ATPase that plays an essential role for many cellular processes in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Cdc48 function in eukaryotes.

claim: An archaeal homologue of Cdc48 was shown to directly interact with the 20S proteasome.
source: An archaeal homologue of this highly conserved enzyme was shown to directly interact with the 20S proteasome.
evidence: This refers to prior research findings about archaeal Cdc48.

claim: Cdc48-like protein of actinobacteria (Cpa) forms hexameric rings.
source: Our data demonstrate that Cdc48-like protein of actinobacteria (Cpa) forms hexameric rings and that the oligomeric state correlates directly with the ATPase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from size exclusion chromatography, SEC-MALS, and electron microscopy presented in the manuscript.

claim: The oligomeric state of Cpa correlates directly with the ATPase activity.
source: Our data demonstrate that Cdc48-like protein of actinobacteria (Cpa) forms hexameric rings and that the oligomeric state correlates directly with the ATPase activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing ATPase activity dependence on assembly conditions.

claim: Assembled Cpa rings can physically interact with the 20S core particle.
source: Furthermore, we show that the assembled Cpa rings can physically interact with the 20S core particle.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial two-hybrid assays, electron microscopy, competition assays, and microscale thermophoresis data.

claim: Comparison of Mycobacterium smegmatis wild-type with a cpa knockout strain under carbon starvation uncovers significant changes in the levels of around 500 proteins.
source: Comparison of the Mycobacterium smegmatis wild-type with a cpa knockout strain under carbon starvation uncovers significant changes in the levels of around 500 proteins.
evidence: This is based on label-free quantification mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pathway mapping of the observed pattern of changes identifies ribosomal proteins as a particular hotspot.
source: Pathway mapping of the observed pattern of changes identifies ribosomal proteins as a particular hotspot, pointing amongst others toward a role of Cpa in ribosome adaptation during starvation.
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis of proteomic data using STRING and DAVID tools.

claim: Cpa may play a role in ribosome adaptation during starvation.
source: Pathway mapping of the observed pattern of changes identifies ribosomal proteins as a particular hotspot, pointing amongst others toward a role of Cpa in ribosome adaptation during starvation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the accumulation of ribosomal proteins in the knockout strain and co-IP results.

claim: Mycobacteria and many other actinobacteria possess several independent chaperone-protease complexes including the canonical bacterial Clp protease system, membrane-bound FtsH protease, and a eukaryotic-like proteasome system.
source: Mycobacteria and many other actinobacteria possess several independent chaperone-protease complexes: the canonical bacterial Clp protease system and membrane-bound FtsH protease as well as a eukaryotic-like proteasome system (Imkamp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The existence of proteasomes in bacteria is an unusual feature restricted to actinobacteria.
source: The existence of proteasomes in bacteria is an unusual feature restricted to actinobacteria, a diverse phylum with different members showing various examples of eukaryotic-like complexes or activities (Cavalier-Smith, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The bacterial 20S proteasome core particle must associate with an activator to form the fully active proteolytic complex.
source: Like in eukaryotes, the bacterial 20S proteasome core particle must associate with an activator to form the fully active proteolytic complex.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about proteasome function.

claim: ARC (also called Mpa in mycobacteria) is a divergent AAA+ family protein that catalyzes the ATP-dependent unfolding and translocation into the proteasome chamber of proteins post-translationally modified with prokaryotic ubiquitin-like protein Pup.
source: The first activator described was ARC (ATPase forming ring-shaped complexes), also called Mpa (mycobacterial proteasomal ATPase) in mycobacteria, a divergent AAA+ family protein that catalyzes the ATP-dependent unfolding and translocation into the proteasome chamber of proteins post-translationally modified with prokaryotic ubiquitin-like protein Pup (Burns et al., 2009; Pearce et al., 2008; Striebel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Proteomic studies on whole-cell purified 'pupylomes' identified hundreds of cellular proteins as pupylation targets.
source: Proteomic studies on whole-cell purified 'pupylomes' (pupylated proteomes) identified hundreds of cellular proteins as pupylation targets (Compton et al., 2015; Festa et al., 2010; Watrous et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior proteomic studies.

claim: Ketopantoate hydroxymethyltransferase (PanB) is one of the best characterized pupylation targets and favorite in vitro substrates.
source: One of the best characterized pupylation targets and favorite in vitro substrates is ketopantoate hydroxymethyltransferase (PanB), the enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step of pantothenate biosynthesis (Chaudhuri et al., 2003; Pearce et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bpa (also referred to as PafE) is a second proteasomal activator that acts in an ATP-independent manner.
source: More recently, a second proteasomal activator was discovered, the bacterial proteasome activator Bpa (also referred to as PafE) (Delley et al., 2014; Jastrab et al., 2015). Bpa acts in an ATP-independent manner and is thought to aid in proteasomal degradation of proteins damaged under stress conditions, since it supports degradation of the unstructured model substrate casein and is involved in degradation of the conformationally unstable transcriptional heat shock protein repressor HspR in vivo (Jastrab et al., 2017; Jastrab et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mpa/ARC and Bpa both form ring-shaped complexes with a central pore.
source: The two non-homologous activators Mpa/ARC and Bpa both form ring-shaped complexes with a central pore and share as one additional important feature with eukaryotic proteasome interactors a C-terminal proteasome interaction motif featuring a penultimate tyrosine (Delley et al., 2014; Imkamp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mpa/ARC and Bpa share a C-terminal proteasome interaction motif featuring a penultimate tyrosine.
source: The two non-homologous activators Mpa/ARC and Bpa both form ring-shaped complexes with a central pore and share as one additional important feature with eukaryotic proteasome interactors a C-terminal proteasome interaction motif featuring a penultimate tyrosine (Delley et al., 2014; Imkamp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In eukaryotes, the HbYX motif features a tyrosine preceded by a hydrophobic residue.
source: In eukaryotes, this motif is called HbYX motif, since the tyrosine is preceded by a hydrophobic residue.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic proteasome interaction motifs.

claim: Mpa/ARC and Bpa both carry the sequence 'GQYL' where Q can be mutated freely without changing association behavior with the proteasome.
source: Mpa/ARC and Bpa on the other hand both carry the sequence 'GQYL', where Q can be mutated freely without changing association behavior of the activator with the proteasome (Jastrab et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In eukaryotes, 20S proteasomes are found in the cytoplasm as well as in the nucleus.
source: In eukaryotes, 20S proteasomes are found in the cytoplasm as well as in the nucleus, where they degrade proteins upon association with the 19S regulatory particle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic proteasome localization.

claim: The eukaryotic 19S regulatory particle contains six ATPase subunits that form the hexameric basal ring stacking onto the 20S cylinder.
source: The regulatory particle contains six ATPase subunits that form the hexameric basal ring stacking onto the 20S cylinder.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic proteasome structure.

claim: The proteasome is responsible for degradation of ER-resident proteins via the ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway that requires retrotranslocation of substrate proteins out of the ER into the cytoplasm.
source: However, the proteasome is also responsible for degradation of ER-resident proteins via the so-called ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway that requires retrotranslocation of substrate proteins out of the ER into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ERAD pathway.

claim: In the ERAD context, the 20S proteasome cooperates with Cdc48 (also known as p97 or VCP).
source: In this context, the 20S proteasome additionally cooperates with another AAA+ protein, Cdc48 (also known as p97 or VCP) (Baek et al., 2013; DeLaBarre et al., 2006; Wolf and Stolz, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cdc48 has been implicated in membrane fusion, autophagy and gene expression.
source: Cdc48 has also been implicated in a multitude of other cellular processes like membrane fusion, autophagy and gene expression (Baek et al., 2013; Yamanaka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Different Cdc48 functions are largely mediated by various adaptor proteins (>40) binding to the N-terminal domain or C-terminal region of Cdc48.
source: The different Cdc48 functions are largely mediated by various adaptor proteins (>40) binding to the N-terminal domain or C-terminal region of Cdc48 and aiding in recognition of different substrates (Baek et al., 2013; Buchberger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent evidence suggests a direct association between Cdc48 and the 20S particle.
source: Although the exact role played by Cdc48 during ERAD is not fully understood, it is involved in pulling proteins from the membrane or from ribosomes during co-translational degradation, and recent evidence suggests even a direct association with the 20S particle (Barthelme and Sauer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Cdc48 homolog from archaea acts as a 20S proteasome activator in vitro.
source: Such a direct role as 20S proteasome activator has been shown for the Cdc48 homolog from archaea in vitro (Barthelme et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Archaeal Cdc48 forms a complex with the 20S proteasome that is capable of degrading ssrA-tagged model substrates.
source: Archaeal Cdc48 forms a complex with the 20S proteasome that is capable of degrading ssrA-tagged model substrates, likely due to the disordered, extended nature of the ssrA-tag at their C-terminus (Barthelme and Sauer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Eukaryotic Cdc48 is not able to recognize ssrA-tagged substrates in vitro due to the absence of two hydrophobic residues in the entry pore loop.
source: Eukaryotic Cdc48 on the other hand is not able to recognize ssrA-tagged substrates in vitro, which was proposed to be due to the absence of two hydrophobic residues in the entry pore loop.
evidence: This is based on inference from prior literature.

claim: Introduction of two hydrophobic residues into the eukaryotic p97 entry pore loop enabled it to unfold ssrA-tagged model substrates.
source: These residues must be involved in recognition of the ssrA tag, since their introduction into the eukaryotic p97 enabled it to unfold ssrA-tagged model substrates (Barthelme and Sauer, 2013; Rothballer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The D1 pore-1 loops and the nature of the residues within these loops play a general role in substrate recruitment.
source: Although the ssrA-tag is not a bona fide degradation signal in eukaryots and archaea, the D1 pore-1 loops and the nature of the residues within these loops appear to play a general role in substrate recruitment.
evidence: This is based on inference from experimental data cited.

claim: Mutating residues in the D1 pore-1 entry loops in vivo deregulated cellular protein turnover.
source: A recent study demonstrated that mutating residues in these entry loops in vivo deregulated cellular protein turnover (Esaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the mammalian Cdc48 homolog, residues in the entry loops are required for proper function of the ERAD pathway.
source: In the mammalian homolog, the same residues are required for proper function of the ERAD pathway (DeLaBarre et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Actinobacterial Cpa orthologs form an independent cluster in the Cdc48-family tree.
source: Interestingly, mycobacterial Rv0435c, as well as its actinobacterial orthologs, form an independent cluster in the Cdc48-family tree (Figure 1A, blue branch).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Sporadically occurring Cdc48 homologs of bacterial species outside of the phylum Actinobacteria cluster with archaeal Cdc48 family members.
source: In contrast, sporadically occurring Cdc48 homologs of bacterial species outside of the phylum Actinobacteria do not cluster with their actinobacterial counterparts, but rather with archaeal Cdc48 family members (Figure 1A, grey branches within the green archaeal branch and lime-green group in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Non-actinobacterial bacteria acquired the cdc48 gene by means of horizontal gene transfer from Archaea.
source: This, in combination with their infrequent occurrence in bacterial genomes would indicate that these bacteria acquired the cdc48 gene by means of horizontal gene transfer from Archaea while the actinobacterial homolog Cpa is a descendant from a common Cdc48 ancestor.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic clustering patterns.

claim: The actinobacterial homolog Cpa is a descendant from a common Cdc48 ancestor.
source: This, in combination with their infrequent occurrence in bacterial genomes would indicate that these bacteria acquired the cdc48 gene by means of horizontal gene transfer from Archaea while the actinobacterial homolog Cpa is a descendant from a common Cdc48 ancestor.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic clustering patterns.

claim: None of the actinobacteria lacking proteasomal subunit genes encode a Cdc48 ortholog.
source: Interestingly, none of the actinobacteria lacking proteasomal subunit genes encode a Cdc48 ortholog.
evidence: This is based on genomic co-occurrence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Where Cpa is present in actinobacteria, it co-occurs with the 20S proteasome.
source: In other words, where Cpa is present in actinobacteria, it co-occurs with the 20S proteasome.
evidence: This is based on genomic co-occurrence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The co-occurrence of Cpa with the 20S proteasome supports the possibility that Cpa could be another proteasomal interactor.
source: This observation supports the possibility that Cpa could be another proteasomal interactor, as it was shown for the eukaryotic and archaeal homologs (Barthelme and Sauer, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on genomic co-occurrence data and comparison to eukaryotic/archaeal homologs.

claim: Cpa features the canonical domain structure of tandem AAA-module proteins with a small N-terminal domain followed by two consecutive canonical AAA modules (D1 and D2).
source: Analysis of the sequence alignment of 76 representative actinobacterial orthologs together with the recently solved crystal structure of the mycobacterial Cpa monomer show that Cpa features the canonical domain structure of tandem AAA-module proteins (Unciuleac et al., 2016). A small N-terminal domain (referred to as N-domain), usually responsible for binding adaptors and/or substrates, is followed by two consecutive canonical AAA modules (D1 and D2, respectively).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis and a cited crystal structure.

claim: Only the D2 module of Cpa carries the sensor asparagine and arginine finger.
source: The AAA modules each contain Walker A and B motifs required for ATP binding and hydrolysis; however, only the D2 module carries the so-called sensor asparagine (assisting the Walker B motif in coordinating water molecules) and arginine finger (stimulating the ATPase activity) (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) (Unciuleac et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis and structural modeling shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The alignment around the Walker A and B motifs shows strict conservation of the motifs in the D2 module, while the D1 module exhibits mild degeneration of the motifs.
source: The alignment around the Walker A and B motifs shows strict conservation of the motifs in the D2 module, while the D1 module exhibits mild degeneration of the motifs (sequence logos in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Actinobacterial Cdc48-like proteins form a separate, tight cluster rather than clustering together with any specific other group.
source: This analysis confirms that actinobacterial Cdc48-like proteins form a separate, tight cluster rather than clustering together with any specific other group (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The N-domains are the main distinguishing feature between the members of the different Cdc48 families, while the ATPase modules are highly conserved across the families.
source: Analysis of the second component loadings, which showcase the separation between the different families, revealed that the N-domains are the main distinguishing feature between the members of the different families, while the ATPase modules are highly conserved across the families (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A crystal structure was recently determined for the Mycobacterium smegmatis Cpa (Msm0858) in its monomeric form.
source: A crystal structure was recently determined for the Mycobacterium smegmatis (Msm) Cpa (Msm0858) in its monomeric form and the study concludes that Msm0858 does not form the canonical hexameric ring structures but rather acts as a monomer in solution (Unciuleac et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a citation to prior literature.

claim: A previous study concluded that Msm0858 does not form the canonical hexameric ring structures but rather acts as a monomer in solution.
source: A crystal structure was recently determined for the Mycobacterium smegmatis (Msm) Cpa (Msm0858) in its monomeric form and the study concludes that Msm0858 does not form the canonical hexameric ring structures but rather acts as a monomer in solution (Unciuleac et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the absence of nucleotide, RerCpa eluted in one main peak at an elution volume equivalent to a monomer/dimer assembly state.
source: In the absence of nucleotide, RerCpa eluted in one main peak at an elution volume equivalent to a monomer/dimer assembly state (Figure 2A, black profile).
evidence: This is based on size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Incubation of RerCpa with ADP-AlFx prior to size exclusion resulted in a shift of the monomer/dimer elution peak to a position equivalent to just above 500 kDa.
source: Incubation of RerCpa with the ATP-hydrolysis transition state analog ADP-AlFx prior to size exclusion resulted in a shift of the monomer/dimer elution peak to a position equivalent to just above 500 kDa (as indicated by the molecular weight standards), which is in good agreement with a hexameric assembly state (expected molecular weight: 450 kDa).
evidence: This is based on size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The light scattering signal revealed the mass of the assembled species in the main peak to correspond to 430 ± 39 kDa.
source: The light scattering signal revealed the mass of the assembled species in the main peak to correspond to 430 ± 39 kDa. This is in good agreement with the molecular weight of six monomers (75 kDa) in a hexameric assembly (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A fraction of RerCpa eluted at an earlier position which corresponds to the molecular weight of a dodecameric assembly (943 kDa) likely due to the high protein concentration.
source: A fraction in Figure 2A eluted at an earlier position which corresponds to the molecular weight of a dodecameric assembly (943 kDa) and is likely due to the high protein concentration which was used for this experiment.
evidence: This is based on SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 2A and is an inference about the cause.

claim: The 2D classification of the imaged Cpa particles revealed that most of the classes represent hexameric assemblies.
source: The 2D classification of the imaged particles revealed that most of the classes represent hexameric assemblies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The diameter of the Cpa particles is roughly 150 Å.
source: Nevertheless, the diameter of the particles is rather uniform with roughly 150 Å and the appearance and dimensions of the particles agree well with hexameric ring assemblies that were observed previously for archaeal or eukaryotic Cdc48.
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy measurements.

claim: The appearance and dimensions of the Cpa particles agree well with hexameric ring assemblies that were observed previously for archaeal or eukaryotic Cdc48.
source: Nevertheless, the diameter of the particles is rather uniform with roughly 150 Å and the appearance and dimensions of the particles agree well with hexameric ring assemblies that were observed previously for archaeal or eukaryotic Cdc48.
evidence: This is based on comparison of electron microscopy data with prior literature.

claim: Mycobacterial Cpa can also form hexameric rings like the rhodococcal protein.
source: To test whether the mycobacterial Cpa can also form hexameric rings like the rhodococcal protein, we repeated the size-exclusion experiment described in the previous paragraph using MsmCpa incubated in the presence of ADP-AlFx (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The elution profile clearly shows that mycobacterial Cpa also forms hexamers in the presence of nucleotide.
evidence: This is based on size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mycobacterial Cpa exhibits low ATPase activity at 28°C.
source: Although mycobacterial Cpa exhibits low ATPase activity at 28°C, we observed a five-fold increase in activity when the temperature was increased to 37°C (change from 7.9 ± 2.9 to 42.5 ± 3.2 min−1 hexamer−1).
evidence: This is based on ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A five-fold increase in ATPase activity of mycobacterial Cpa was observed when the temperature was increased from 28°C to 37°C.
source: Although mycobacterial Cpa exhibits low ATPase activity at 28°C, we observed a five-fold increase in activity when the temperature was increased to 37°C (change from 7.9 ± 2.9 to 42.5 ± 3.2 min−1 hexamer−1).
evidence: This is based on ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The rhodococcal Cpa exhibited a strong dependence of its ATPase activity on both pH and KCl concentration.
source: The rhodococcal Cpa exhibited a strong dependence of its ATPase activity on both, pH and KCl concentration, where increasing pH and decreasing salt concentration led to an increase in the measured enzyme activity by up to sevenfold (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Increasing pH and decreasing salt concentration led to an increase in the measured Cpa enzyme activity by up to sevenfold.
source: The rhodococcal Cpa exhibited a strong dependence of its ATPase activity on both, pH and KCl concentration, where increasing pH and decreasing salt concentration led to an increase in the measured enzyme activity by up to sevenfold (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Increasing the salt concentration from 0 to 400 mM led to a strong deceleration of Cpa ring formation.
source: Interestingly, increasing the salt concentration from 0 to 400 mM led to a strong deceleration of ring formation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on time-resolved size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When no salt was present in the sample the oligomerization was complete within a few minutes.
source: When no salt was present in the sample the oligomerization was complete within a few minutes, while at the highest KCl concentration only 40% of Cpa was assembled into rings after 5 hr of incubation.
evidence: This is based on time-resolved size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At the highest KCl concentration only 40% of Cpa was assembled into rings after 5 hr of incubation.
source: When no salt was present in the sample the oligomerization was complete within a few minutes, while at the highest KCl concentration only 40% of Cpa was assembled into rings after 5 hr of incubation.
evidence: This is based on time-resolved size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The measured ATPase activity reports mainly on the protein assembly state and indicates that ring formation is strongly dependent on ionic strength.
source: This result indicates that during the time frame in which the ATPase assay is performed the assembly is still slowly ongoing with its velocity dependent on the initial KCl concentration. Therefore, the measured activity reports mainly on the protein assembly state and indicates that ring formation is indeed strongly dependent on ionic strength.
evidence: This is an inference based on the assembly kinetics and ATPase activity data.

claim: The activity of around 60 pmol 4-methylumbelliferone produced per min per OD unit indicates that the full-length mycobacterial Cpa is capable of directly interacting with the proteasomal core particle in the context of a bacterial cell.
source: The activity of around 60 pmol 4-methylumbelliferone produced per min per OD unit indicates that the full-length mycobacterial Cpa is capable of directly interacting with the proteasomal core particle in the context of a bacterial cell.
evidence: This is based on bacterial two-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Removal of the C-terminal amino acids does not change the interaction strength between Cpa and the 20S core particle.
source: Additionally, we observe that removal of the C-terminal amino acids does not change the interaction strength between Cpa and the 20S core particle, indicating that those residues do not significantly mediate this interaction.
evidence: This is based on bacterial two-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A small fraction of coaxial Cpa-proteasome complexes in side view were observed in negatively stained EM micrographs.
source: We observed a small fraction of coaxial Cpa-proteasome complexes in side view (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, white arrows) next to uncapped 20S cylinders (Figure 4C, yellow arrows) and free Cpa rings (Figure 4C, blue arrows).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of RerCpa, pupylated ketopanthoate hydroxymethyltransferase (MtbPanB-Pup) is completely degraded within 20 min under the assay conditions.
source: In the absence of RerCpa, pupylated ketopanthoate hydroxymethyltransferase (MtbPanB-Pup), a well-characterized degradation substrate of the MtbMpa-20S complex, is completely degraded within 20 min under the assay conditions, while in the presence of RerCpa no significant degradation takes place within the same time frame (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on degradation assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the presence of RerCpa no significant degradation of MtbPanB-Pup takes place within 20 min.
source: In the absence of RerCpa, pupylated ketopanthoate hydroxymethyltransferase (MtbPanB-Pup), a well-characterized degradation substrate of the MtbMpa-20S complex, is completely degraded within 20 min under the assay conditions, while in the presence of RerCpa no significant degradation takes place within the same time frame (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on degradation assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RerCpa could inhibit degradation of Pup-GFP by the RerARC-20S complex in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Like in the heterologous setup, RerCpa could inhibit degradation of Pup-GFP by the RerARC-20S complex in a concentration-dependent manner, indicating interaction between Cpa and the 20S proteasome.
evidence: This is based on degradation assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In presence of ATP, a dissociation constant of 0.36 ± 0.02 μM was measured for the interaction between Cpa and closed-gate proteasome.
source: In presence of ATP, we measured a dissociation constant of 0.36 ± 0.02 μM for the closed-gate proteasome and 0.56 ± 0.05 μM for the open-gate proteasome, indicating that the interaction between Cpa and closed-gate core particle is marginally stronger than with the open-gate variant.
evidence: This is based on microscale thermophoresis data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In presence of ATP, a dissociation constant of 0.56 ± 0.05 μM was measured for the interaction between Cpa and open-gate proteasome.
source: In presence of ATP, we measured a dissociation constant of 0.36 ± 0.02 μM for the closed-gate proteasome and 0.56 ± 0.05 μM for the open-gate proteasome, indicating that the interaction between Cpa and closed-gate core particle is marginally stronger than with the open-gate variant.
evidence: This is based on microscale thermophoresis data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The interaction between Cpa and closed-gate core particle is marginally stronger than with the open-gate variant.
source: In presence of ATP, we measured a dissociation constant of 0.36 ± 0.02 μM for the closed-gate proteasome and 0.56 ± 0.05 μM for the open-gate proteasome, indicating that the interaction between Cpa and closed-gate core particle is marginally stronger than with the open-gate variant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of dissociation constants measured by microscale thermophoresis.

claim: No signal change was observed in absence of ATP, demonstrating that the measured interaction is specific to the Cpa hexamer that is formed only when nucleotide is present.
source: Importantly, we could not observe a signal change in absence of ATP, demonstrating that the measured interaction is specific to the Cpa hexamer that is formed only when nucleotide is present.
evidence: This is based on microscale thermophoresis data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The knockout strain exhibited no growth defect compared to the parent strain under standard culture conditions.
source: The knockout strain exhibited no growth defect compared to the parent strain under standard culture conditions (Middlebrook 7H9 medium with glycerol and Tween 80 at 37°C) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on growth curve data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Transfer of the parent and knockout strain cultures to a medium devoid of glycerol reveals a growth defect in the knockout strain.
source: However, transfer of the parent and knockout strain cultures grown in minimal medium supplemented with glycerol (adapted from (Elharar et al., 2014)) to a medium devoid of glycerol as the main carbon source reveals a growth defect in the knockout strain (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on growth curve data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The wild-type Msm cells undergo two to three divisions during the first 72 hr after transfer to carbon starvation medium.
source: The wild-type Msm cells undergo two to three divisions during the first 72 hr after transfer, while the Msm ∆cpa cells stop dividing already after 24 hr.
evidence: This is based on growth curve data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The Msm ∆cpa cells stop dividing already after 24 hr in carbon starvation medium.
source: The wild-type Msm cells undergo two to three divisions during the first 72 hr after transfer, while the Msm ∆cpa cells stop dividing already after 24 hr.
evidence: This is based on growth curve data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Once cell division has ceased, both strains can persist for at least 2 weeks and can be recovered when plated on 7H10 solid medium.
source: Once cell division has ceased, both strains can persist for at least 2 weeks and can be recovered when plated on 7H10 solid medium (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations mentioned but not shown.

claim: The growth defect result might point to a role of Cpa in adaptation of Msm to nutrient starvation stress.
source: This result might point to a role of Cpa in adaptation of Msm to nutrient starvation stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the growth defect observed under carbon starvation.

claim: In branches 1 and 2 of the actinobacterial cdc48 homolog cluster, cpa is encoded in a putative operon together with psd and pssA.
source: Careful investigation of the genomic context in the three branches shows that in branches 1 and 2 (Figure 1A and B) cpa is encoded in a putative operon together with two other genes: psd (phosphatidylserine decarboxylase proenzyme) and pssA (phosphatidylserine synthase), two consecutively acting enzymes responsible for the synthesis of phosphatidylethanolamine from CDP-diacylglycerol and serine.
evidence: This is based on genomic context analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Psd and pssA are two consecutively acting enzymes responsible for the synthesis of phosphatidylethanolamine from CDP-diacylglycerol and serine.
source: Careful investigation of the genomic context in the three branches shows that in branches 1 and 2 (Figure 1A and B) cpa is encoded in a putative operon together with two other genes: psd (phosphatidylserine decarboxylase proenzyme) and pssA (phosphatidylserine synthase), two consecutively acting enzymes responsible for the synthesis of phosphatidylethanolamine from CDP-diacylglycerol and serine.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of these enzymes.

claim: In the genomes of branches 1 and 2, the proteasomal genes are usually located within a relatively fixed distance from the cpa locus.
source: In the genomes of those two branches, the proteasomal genes are usually located within a relatively fixed distance from the cpa locus.
evidence: This is based on genomic context analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the actinobacteria belonging to the third branch, the psd/pssA genes exist, but are not located in the same operon as or in close proximity of the cpa gene.
source: In the actinobacteria belonging to the third branch, the psd/pssA genes exist, but are not located in the same operon as or in close proximity of the cpa gene.
evidence: This is based on genomic context analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The psd, pssA and cpa genes are expressed together from a polycistronic operon.
source: Consistent with a single mRNA generated from the three genes, all six amplification products were present: two probes spanning joints between psd/pssA and pssA/cpa (probes A and B), a cpa-specific probe (probe C) as well as three longer probes, spanning two or three genes at the same time (probes D, E and F). Evidently, the psd, pssA and cpa genes are expressed together from a polycistronic operon.
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Phosphatidylethanolamine has been implicated in membrane curvature determination as well as cell division in some organisms.
source: Considering that phosphatidylethanolamine has been implicated in membrane curvature determination as well as cell division in some organisms (Mileykovskaya et al., 1998) and that the genes responsible for its synthesis are co-expressed with the cpa gene, we were interested to see whether removal of Cpa from the cell would influence the shape of starved cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The knockout cells were longer by approximately 13% compared to the wild-type cells under carbon starvation.
source: The knockout cells were longer by approximately 13% compared to the wild-type cells.
evidence: This is based on light microscopy measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: 45 proteins during normal growth and 251 proteins during carbon starvation were at least 1.5 times more abundant in the wild type strain compared to Msm ∆cpa.
source: We observed 45 proteins during normal growth and 251 proteins during carbon starvation that were at least 1.5 times more abundant in the wild type strain compared to Msm ∆cpa.
evidence: This is based on label-free quantification mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: 49 proteins were found to accumulate in the knockout cells during normal growth and 254 proteins during carbon starvation compared to Msm wt.
source: Likewise, 49 proteins were found to accumulate in the knockout cells during normal growth and 254 proteins during carbon starvation compared to Msm wt.
evidence: This is based on label-free quantification mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: While during standard growth the differences are rather mild, exposing the cells to starvation stress led to significantly higher accumulation or depletion of a larger number of proteins in the cpa knockout strain.
source: Consequently, while during standard growth the differences are rather mild, exposing the cells to starvation stress led to significantly higher accumulation or depletion of a larger number of proteins in the cpa knockout strain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of proteomic changes under different conditions.

claim: This observation strengthens the notion of Cpa playing a role during adaptation to nutrient-limited conditions.
source: This observation strengthens the notion of Cpa playing a role during adaptation to nutrient-limited conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic changes observed under starvation.

claim: In both cases (cells starved and non-starved), the class with most of the changed proteins was 'transcription'.
source: We observed that in both cases (cells starved and non-starved), the class with most of the changed proteins was 'transcription'.
evidence: This is based on COG classification analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Many changes occurred in classes like 'transcription', 'energy production and conversion', 'amino acid transport and metabolism' and 'lipid transport and metabolism' when the cells were starved for carbon.
source: We found that many changes occurred in classes like 'transcription' (most represented, similarly to standard growth), 'energy production and conversion', 'amino acid transport and metabolism' and 'lipid transport and metabolism'.
evidence: This is based on COG classification analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The pathway enrichment analysis showed an unusually high number of structural components of the ribosome accumulating in the cpa-knockout cells.
source: The result of this analysis showed an unusually high number of structural components of the ribosome (Figure 9—figure supplements 1 and 2) accumulating in the cpa-knockout cells.
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis using STRING and DAVID tools, shown in Figure 9—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: COG class J, encompassing proteins connected to translation and ribosome, was one of the very few classes that contained mostly proteins accumulating in the knockout cells and few with decreased levels.
source: In fact, COG class J, encompassing proteins connected to translation and ribosome, was one of the very few classes that contained mostly proteins accumulating in the knockout cells and few with decreased levels (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on COG classification analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Archaeal Cdc48-CP assembly is capable of degrading an ssrA-tagged model substrate in vitro.
source: Similarly, although the archaeal Cdc48-CP assembly is capable of degrading an ssrA-tagged model substrate in vitro, archaea do not harbor the tmRNA, a crucial element of trans-translation encoding the ssrA-tag (Hayes and Keiler, 2010; Karzai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Archaea do not harbor the tmRNA, a crucial element of trans-translation encoding the ssrA-tag.
source: Similarly, although the archaeal Cdc48-CP assembly is capable of degrading an ssrA-tagged model substrate in vitro, archaea do not harbor the tmRNA, a crucial element of trans-translation encoding the ssrA-tag (Hayes and Keiler, 2010; Karzai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Actinobacteria feature a tmRNA and carry out trans-translation.
source: Actinobacteria feature a tmRNA and carry out trans-translation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about actinobacteria.

claim: No Cpa-mediated degradation of ssrA-tagged model substrates could be detected in vitro.
source: However, no Cpa-mediated degradation of ssrA-tagged model substrates could be detected in vitro (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations mentioned but not shown.

claim: The Clp protease system is responsible for ssrA-tagged substrate degradation in mycobacteria and related bacteria.
source: As the Clp protease system is responsible for ssrA-tagged substrate degradation in mycobacteria and related bacteria, this finding was not unexpected (Laederach et al., 2014; Raju et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cdc48 family members almost always act in the context of adaptor proteins.
source: The search for substrates is likely further hampered by the fact that Cdc48 family members almost always act in the context of adaptor proteins.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Cdc48 function.

claim: In the absence of adaptor proteins, the activity toward the adaptor-mediated set of substrates is not detectable.
source: In the absence of these adaptors, the activity toward the adaptor-mediated set of substrates is simply not detectable.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge about Cdc48 function.

claim: Several studies indicate a functional link between phosphatidylethanolamine and cytokinesis, both in eukaryotes and bacteria.
source: Several studies indicate a functional link between phosphatidylethanolamine and cytokinesis, both in eukaryotes and bacteria (Luo et al., 2009; Mileykovskaya et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Removal of Cpa from the cells did not show a significant effect on cell division as gauged by their cell size and morphology.
source: Removal of Cpa from the cells did not, however, show a significant effect on cell division as gauged by their cell size and morphology.
evidence: This is based on light microscopy observations shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: In other bacteria it has been observed that nutrient stress (carbon starvation among others) results in ribosome disassembly and rRNA degradation.
source: In other bacteria it has been observed that nutrient stress (carbon starvation among others) results in ribosome disassembly and rRNA degradation (Zundel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: An excess of ribosomal proteins is removed from yeast cells by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: Additionally, another recent study reported that an excess of ribosomal proteins is removed from yeast cells by the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Sung et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Actinobacterial Cpa may be involved in disassembly and/or removal of ribosomal proteins under nutrient limitation.
source: It is tempting to hypothesise that actinobacterial Cpa is involved in a similar process; however, more effort will be required to investigate whether the role played by Cpa in disassembly and/or removal of ribosomal proteins under nutrient limitation requires cooperation with the proteasome core or is mainly mediated by its AAA pore-threading activity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the proteomic data and comparison to other systems.

claim: Eukaryotic Cdc48 is implicated in processing of ubiquitinated proteins.
source: For example, eukaryotic Cdc48 is implicated in processing of ubiquitinated proteins (Richly et al., 2005; Rumpf and Jentsch, 2006), a post-translational modification that does not occur in actinobacteria.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ubiquitination does not occur in actinobacteria.
source: For example, eukaryotic Cdc48 is implicated in processing of ubiquitinated proteins (Richly et al., 2005; Rumpf and Jentsch, 2006), a post-translational modification that does not occur in actinobacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about actinobacteria.

claim: Actinobacteria possess the functionally analogous covalent modifier Pup that renders proteins as substrates for degradation by the Mpa-proteasome complex.
source: Actinobacteria possess, however, the functionally analogous covalent modifier Pup that renders proteins as substrates for degradation by the Mpa-proteasome complex (Striebel et al., 2010; Striebel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The well-characterized pupylation substrate PanB accumulates in the cpa-knockout strain.
source: The well-characterized pupylation substrate PanB in fact accumulates in the cpa-knockout strain.
evidence: This is based on proteomic data from the manuscript.

claim: In vitro degradation tests with recombinantly produced and in vitro pupylated PanB showed no degradation in presence of Cpa and the proteasome.
source: However, in vitro degradation tests with recombinantly produced and in vitro pupylated PanB showed no degradation in presence of Cpa and the proteasome (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations mentioned but not shown.

claim: Cpa forms hexameric rings, their assembly strongly dependent on pH and ionic strength.
source: We show that Cpa forms hexameric rings, their assembly strongly dependent on pH and ionic strength.
evidence: This is based on size exclusion chromatography and assembly kinetics data.

claim: Once formed, the Cpa rings are capable of interacting with the proteasomal core particle, identifying Cpa as a novel proteasomal interactor in actinobacteria.
source: Once formed, the rings are capable of interacting with the proteasomal core particle, identifying Cpa as a novel proteasomal interactor in actinobacteria.
evidence: This is based on multiple interaction assays including two-hybrid, EM, competition assays, and MST.
